summary: A 1970 specification for network use of the UCSB On-Line System. It was updated by RFC 217 and RFC 225.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes how a network user could connect to the UCSB On-Line System. It explains the login handoff and the streams used to send keyboard input and receive display output.

subtitle: Explains how remote users connected to the UCSB On-Line System through its network interface.

tldr.problem: Network users needed documented instructions for opening a session with the UCSB On-Line System and exchanging its input and display data.
tldr.mechanism: A user connects to the system's primary socket, receives a socket number, and then establishes separate input and output connections to the Interface.
tldr.outcome: The memo specifies the connection sequence and record formats for several output classes. Unit metadata lists RFCs 217 and 225 as updates.

today: RFC 74 is an early specification for using the UCSB On-Line System, and the unit metadata lists RFCs 217 and 225 as updates to it.

sections.title: The On-Line System Interface
sections.content:
The UCSB On-Line System (OLS) is available to network users through an intermediary process called the Interface. The Interface is reached at the system's primary socket and communicates through the Network Control Program.

This memo is for programmers who need to communicate with the Interface. It is not a user manual for OLS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Network users connect to an Interface process that passes input to OLS and returns its output. The memo explains the interface for programmers, not how to use OLS as a person.

sections.title: Logging In and Opening Connections
sections.content:
A user requests a connection to OLS's primary socket. If the Interface is not already active, the Logger rejects the first request, loads the Interface, and dispatches it; the user then retries. A second rejection means the system or its resources are unavailable.

The Interface sends a socket number and closes the initial connection. It then establishes two connections with the user: one for input and one for output. The Interface considers the user logged in once both connections are established.
sections.plainLanguage: The first connection starts or finds the Interface. After a socket handoff, the user opens separate connections for sending keys and receiving displays.

sections.title: Input and Output Data
sections.content:
The input connection carries one-byte key codes as a continuous stream. The Interface forwards them to OLS, which processes them like keyboard input. The second input byte selects which classes of OLS output the Interface should suppress.

The output connection carries variable-length records for alphanumeric, curvilinear, and special-character output. Each record identifies its output class and includes class-specific information, data, and a length field.
sections.plainLanguage: Input arrives as key codes, while output arrives as records describing text or graphic data. A user can disable output types that their terminal cannot display.

sections.title: Ending a Session
sections.content:
The two input and output connections remain open while the user is logged in. The user is expected to close both connections when finished, which makes the local sockets available again.

The memo warns users to send the OLS sign-off key before ending the network connection. Otherwise, a later network user could find that session still logged in.
sections.plainLanguage: Close both network connections when leaving OLS. Sign off from OLS first so that the next network user does not inherit the session.
